source.title: Constitutional adapters: Inference-time interventions for misalignment and misuse

record.tranche_reason: The study constructs a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction using the cited method, applies it as an additive steering intervention, and reports refusal-related behavior and capability outcomes on a new model. It does not report the direction-ablation intervention.
record.gate_note: The refusal-direction candidates' ablation, induction, and KL scores were used to select a layer and position; they are not reported as outcome results and are not rows. The paper evaluates additive refusal steering at α = 0.3. Results for other interventions are not recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study's harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means baseline follows Arditi et al. It is added at every position (α = 0.3) on Qwen3.5-4B, a new hybrid Gated-DeltaNet architecture. The study reports its effect on refusal of jailbroken harmful requests, refusal of benign prompts and capabilities, which bears on V1's 'adding it induces refusal, abilities kept' part. Ablation is used only to select the direction, and no ablation outcome is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors use difference-in-means refusal steering as a simple baseline. It defends well against static and multi-query jailbreaks and stays robust to long padding. It is also surprisingly effective on Petri and agentic misalignment. It largely fails on multi-turn jailbreaks, where difference objects are over 3× more effective. Its over-refusal cost is comparable to the CAs, and the authors claim nothing about ablation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and the cited selection procedure, but evaluates additive steering at α = 0.3 on Qwen3.5-4B rather than reporting the original ablation intervention; the selected vector is applied at every inference position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by attack benchmark: additive refusal steering has large reported gains on static and multi-query attacks, and smaller gains on multi-turn attacks where the unsteered baseline is already highly defended.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal steering reduced agentic leaking misalignment by 31.3 pp and raised Petri misalignment-reduction scores, e.g. +5.8 on delusion/sycophancy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding the refusal direction also suppresses non-refusal misaligned behaviours such as leaking and sycophancy.

fits_no_version.finding: The layer-12 refusal direction is near-orthogonal (cosine about 0) to the learned constitutional and control ReLU read/write directions (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constitution-following steering directions are geometrically distinct from the difference-in-means refusal direction.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and synthetic data will be uploaded pending acceptance
record.problems: The reported refusal-direction behavioral outcomes are for one model. There is no direct ablation outcome, and the direction is applied additively; the study therefore does not establish the full causal-mediation claim.

untested.parts: Ablation removing refusal (computed only as a selection score, not reported); induction at the original α = 1; models other than Qwen3.5-4B (the refusal steer is absent from the Appendix D model comparisons).
No weight-orthogonalization or abliteration evaluation of the target model (an abliterated model is used only as the attacker).
No test of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training against ablation.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
The base-to-instruct transfer concerns constitutional adapters, not the refusal direction, which is fitted on the instruct model.
Jailbreaks are run with thinking off; GSM8K with thinking on is only a capability check.

missing.what: Dose ladder for the refusal steer at α ∈ {0.15, 0.3, 0.5}: defense versus benign-compliance frontier
Refusal steer defense on Pliny with 0–65,536 padding tokens; it stays robust across context lengths
Petri cyber/bio/chem uplift for the refusal steer: +1.7 ±1.6 reduction in misalignment score

record.verdict_notes: The refusal steer is a baseline, and its results are reported as other-method numbers in Tables 4–10. They still measure V1's additive-induction effect in a new architecture, hence T3 rather than T1. α = 0.3 was tuned to keep XSTest over-refusal near 10 pp, so weak benign induction is by design. Several 'absolute' baselines in the record cannot be defense or compliance rates because the steered value would exceed 100% or fall below 0%. They are probably attack-success and over-refusal rates; this should be checked against Figure 12.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report ablating the selected direction or test whether ablation removes refusal. It reports additive steering and associated behavior, not a separate direct test of the direction's causal mediation.
No refusal-direction weight edit or abliteration evaluation.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
The transfer experiments concern the paper's constitutional adapters, not transfer of the difference-in-means refusal direction.
Does not vary refusal training to test when a removable direction exists.
Does not test the claim in reasoning models. GSM8K is run with thinking enabled, but that is a capability evaluation, not a test of refusal-direction mediation in reasoning models.

relationships.condition: Additive refusal direction on Qwen3.5-4B (α = 0.3), static and multi-query jailbreaks, benign over-refusal and capabilities
relationships.reason: Addition raised harmful-request defense by 19–52 pp (r1–r6) and increased refusal of benign prompts by 10–17 pp (r9–r10). MMLU, GSM8K, BCB and BFCL changes stayed within about 2 pp (r11–r14).
relationships.display_finding: Addition improved harmful-request defense by 19–52 percentage points and increased benign refusal by 10–17 points, while MMLU, GSM8K, BCB, and BFCL changed by at most about 2 points.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Additive refusal direction on Qwen3.5-4B (α = 0.3), static and multi-query jailbreaks, benign over-refusal and capabilities
source_check.reason: Defense rises 19.3–51.8 pp (r1–r6), benign refusal rises 10.1 and 16.6 pp (r9–r10), and MMLU/GSM8K/BCB/BFCL changes are within 2 pp with CIs spanning 0 (r11–r14). The weak XSTest induction reflects the deliberately low dose, not a scope failure.

relationships.condition: Multi-turn adaptive jailbreaks (Crescendo, ActorAttack) on Qwen3.5-4B at α = 0.3
relationships.reason: Induced defense was only +8.3 and +6.9 pp despite large headroom (the undefended model was apparently jailbroken about 95–99% of the time). The authors say refusal steering fails against multi-turn jailbreaks (r7–r8).
relationships.display_finding: Defense improved by only 8.3 and 6.9 percentage points against Crescendo and ActorAttack, despite undefended jailbreak success of approximately 95–99%.

labels.condition: Multi-turn adaptive jailbreaks (Crescendo, ActorAttack) on Qwen3.5-4B at α = 0.3
labels.reason: +8.3 ±3.6 and +6.9 ±4.3 pp, against undefended ASR of 99.2% and 95.0% (r7–r8). The effect is present but weak, so not challenges. The Figure 4 caption says refusal steering does not succeed against multi-turn jailbreaks.

relation.reason: The refusal direction is a baseline, but the study reports its own rates for it on jailbreak defense, benign refusal and capabilities. These bear on V1's adding-induces-refusal and abilities-kept parts.

tranche.reason: It uses Arditi's direction extraction and activation addition, but in a new setting (hybrid Gated-DeltaNet Qwen3.5-4B, jailbreak defense, over-refusal benchmarks) with different measures (StrongREJECT defense success). Ablation is used only for selection. T1 does not fit.

source_check.notes: The 'unsteered (absolute)' columns hold undefended attack success rates in Tables 4–6 and over-refusal (refusal) rates in Table 9, so every r1–r10 baseline and the r7/r8 ceiling notes need relabelling. Refusal steering was run only on Qwen3.5-4B, at one layer (block 12, position −5), and ablation was never evaluated as a result. In authors_conclusion, 'surprisingly effective' fits Petri; on agentic misalignment, constitution and difference objects outperformed refusal steering.

statements.correction: Qwen3.5-4B, refusal direction added at α = 0.3: Crescendo +8.3 ±3.6 pp and ActorAttack +6.9 ±4.3 pp defense success, from undefended attack success of 99.2% and 95.0%. The effect is weak but present, so it limits scope rather than challenges. Refusal steering at α ∈ {0.15, 0.3, 0.5} was Pareto-dominated by difference LoRAs on multi-turn attacks.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but listing this study under 'challenges' with 'the direction does not mediate the outcome' overstates it. The effect is small but non-zero (both CIs exclude 0). The study's own verdict is limits_scope, and it tests only addition, not ablation or mediation of the attack.

reader_labels.condition: Additive refusal-vector steering on Qwen3.5-4B at α = 0.3
reader_labels.reason: Steering increased defense success on the reported harmful-request attacks and decreased compliance on benign prompts, while the reported capability changes were small; rows r1–r6 and r9–r14.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Multi-turn attacks on Qwen3.5-4B at α = 0.3
reader_labels.reason: Defense gains were smaller on multi-turn attacks than on the other reported attacks, with the undefended baseline already having high defense success; rows r7–r8.
